title: Carriers strike Manila Bay

facts.text: On 5 and 6 November 1944, two weeks after the Battle of Leyte Gulf, U.S. Navy carrier planes struck Japanese airfields on Luzon and shipping in Manila Bay.
The raids came from Task Force 38, the fast carrier force that Vice Adm. John S. McCain had taken command of on 30 October 1944.
The goal was to wreck the Japanese air power on Luzon that was feeding planes, including kamikaze suicide planes, into the fight for Leyte.
The new carrier USS Ticonderoga (CV-14) launched her first strike on the morning of 5 November, hitting airfields and shipping around Manila.
A Navy combat cameraman aboard Ticonderoga filmed the day's strike; his film slate reads "Combat Photo Unit No. 12, D. R. Brown, CV-14 / Manila, 11/5/44."
The Japanese heavy cruiser Nachi, which had been Vice Adm. Kiyohide Shima's flagship at Surigao Strait, tried to flee Manila Bay at high speed when the raids began.
Planes from the carrier USS Essex hit Nachi first, and planes from USS Lexington (CV-16) finished her that afternoon with bombs, rockets and torpedoes.
Nachi broke into three pieces and sank in Manila Bay near Corregidor. About 807 of her crew were killed and about 220 survived.
Admiral Shima was ashore at a staff conference that morning and watched from land as his flagship was blown apart.
That afternoon a burning Japanese plane carrying a bomb crashed into Lexington's island, wrecking most of it and spraying fire in all directions.
Lexington's crew had the major fires under control within about 20 minutes, and her gunners shot down another kamikaze diving at Ticonderoga.
About 50 of Lexington's men were killed and more than 120 wounded, the worst single loss in the ship's long career.
The carriers came back to Manila on 13 and 14 November and sank the light cruiser Kiso and four destroyers.
In spring 1945, Navy divers from the rescue ship USS Chanticleer made 296 dives on Nachi's wreck and brought up secret documents, radar gear and maps of Japanese defenses on Luzon.

declassified.fact: Vice Adm. John S. McCain, whose carriers struck Manila Bay, stood in the front row of senior officers at the Japanese surrender aboard USS Missouri on 2 September 1945. Four days later he died of a heart attack in Coronado, California, after a welcome home party. In 1949 Congress promoted him to full admiral.

film.shot_notes: U.S. Navy film titled 'Air strikes on Manila harbor, planes in formation, Japanese ships burn'. The catalog record is undated, but the cameraman's slate in the film (6:20 to 6:30 of the NARA file) reads 'Combat Photo Unit No. 12, D. R. Brown, CV-14 / Manila, 11/5/44, roll 9', so USS Ticonderoga, 5 November 1944. The clip is ALREADY CUT, chosen by Brian on 28 Oct: footage/1944-11-05-manila.mp4, 15.8 s, 720 x 412 (the burned in NARA timecode cropped off the bottom), with music under it. Shots from the NARA file: 2:43.7 to 2:48.0 Helldivers banking and peeling off (the opener, motion); 2:56.6 to 2:59.0 the burning shoreline from the air; 3:01.5 to 3:03.4 a bomb burst on the target; 3:04.0 to 3:08.0 flak bursts around the planes; 5:58.3 to 6:01.5 a damaged Helldiver tipped on its nose on Ticonderoga's deck, crew around it. The longer stretch 1:25 to 6:15 (silent, re-encoded at 30 fps) is footage/1944-11-05-manila-reel.mp4 if a recut is needed: carrier from the air at 0:36 to 0:47, Helldiver close up at 1:33 to 1:40, four Helldivers in formation at 1:59 to 2:11.
film.audio: MUSIC, by Brian's decision on 28 Oct 2026 (an exception to the Videos doc's no music rule, for this video only): 'War Epic' by Paul Yudin (Pixabay file paulyudin-war-epic-182501.mp3), supplied by Brian as free use. Copy: footage/1944-11-05-manila-music-paulyudin-war-epic.mp3. The clip uses 0:46.3 to 1:02.1 of the track (starting on the big hit), faded in over 0.3 s and out over the last 1.5 s, and mixed LOW in the background at about -28 LUFS at Brian's request on 29 Oct (do not renormalize it up to -16 LUFS). The film itself is silent. Keep the clip's audio (sound true); do not tag the video as period sound; themes.video.sound should be the closest allowed value and a note added.
